title: The issue management process
blurb: Log and analyse an issue, escalate it to the sponsor and assign actions through to closure, and tell an issue from a risk or a day-to-day problem.
question: Halfway through building a hospital car park, the steel supplier goes into administration. A replacement supplier will add £180,000 and six weeks, well beyond the project manager's tolerances. What should the project manager do, in what order, and why?

teach.h: An issue is a problem the PM cannot absorb
teach.body: Formally, an issue is a problem that is now breaching, or is about to breach, the tolerances delegated to the project manager, so it needs the sponsor's support to resolve. In plain English: something has already gone wrong (or certainly will), and it is too big for the PM to fix within their own authority. Smaller problems that fit inside tolerance are handled by the PM day to day; they are not escalated as issues.

teach.caption: A threat that occurs becomes an issue if it breaches tolerance. Many issues were never identified as risks at all.

steps.label:
Logging and
analysis
steps.sub: Record it; assess impact, urgency, cause and options

steps.label: Escalation
steps.sub: Beyond tolerance: raise to the sponsor with a recommendation

steps.label:
Assignment
of actions
steps.sub: Owners, actions and dates; change control if the baseline moves

steps.label:
Track to
closure
steps.sub: Monitor actions, close when resolved, capture lessons

teach.caption: The PMQ syllabus names the first three stages. Tracking actions to closure completes the job.

teach.body: Logging creates one auditable record, so nothing is forgotten and repeat problems show up as patterns. Analysis gives the decision maker facts: impact on time, cost, quality, scope and benefits, urgency, root cause and options. Escalation puts the decision with someone who has the authority to make it. Assigning actions turns that decision into named, dated work, so the issue is actually resolved. Skip any stage and issues drift, grow and surprise the board.

head: Field
Car park example
teach.caption: A typical log, not a mandated APM format. It is updated until the issue is closed.

root.label: A problem arises
root.sub: Log it and analyse the impact

teach.caption: The test is authority, not how worrying the problem feels.

teach.body: On the car park, the PM's tolerance is £50,000 and two weeks, so the £180,000, six-week problem is an issue. The PM escalates the same day with options: fund it from management reserve, descope the electric-vehicle canopy, or accept a later handover. The sponsor chooses a mix and the descoping goes through change control. Actions follow: procurement signs the new supplier by Friday and the planner rebaselines. Waiting would only have shrunk the options.

teach.h: Issues in linear and iterative projects

rows.label: First resolved by
values: The team, within the time box

teach.caption: Iterative teams surface problems daily, so most are cleared fast. Threats to the fixed time or cost still go up the line.

teach.text: Exam traps: (1) An uncertain future event is a RISK, not an issue. (2) Not every problem is an issue: problems within the PM's tolerance are handled day to day. (3) Never 'convert an issue into a risk' to watch it later: it has happened and needs action now. (4) An issue is not closed when it is escalated or when actions are planned, only when it is resolved.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define an issue: a problem breaching (or about to breach) the PM's tolerances, needing the sponsor.
Logging and analysis: record it, then assess impact, urgency, cause and options.
Escalation: raise it promptly to the sponsor with a recommendation, because the PM lacks the authority.
Assignment of actions: named owners and deadlines, with change control if the baseline changes.
Track actions to closure and capture lessons so it does not recur.
Issue: a problem beyond the PM's tolerances that needs the sponsor's support.
Process: logging and analysis, escalation, assignment of actions, then closure.
Escalate early and bring options plus a recommendation.
Within tolerance it is a day-to-day problem, handled by the PM.
Linear: formal log and change control. Iterative: impediments cleared by the team, with escalation to the product owner or sponsor.

summary: You can now define an issue, explain the purpose of logging and analysis, escalation and assignment of actions, and show why skipping a stage makes things worse. You can also decide whether a problem stays with the PM or goes to the sponsor, in linear and iterative projects.

A.q: Which statement best describes an issue in project management?
options: An uncertain event that may affect objectives
A problem breaching the PM's delegated tolerances
Any task running later than its planned finish date
A request to change the agreed project baseline
A.why: An issue is a problem that is breaching, or about to breach, the tolerances delegated to the project manager, so it needs the sponsor's support.

whyNot.0: An uncertain event that may affect objectives is a risk, not an issue.
whyNot.2: A late task may be well within float or tolerance, so it is not automatically an issue.
whyNot.3: A request to change the baseline is a change request, handled by change control.

A.q: On a website rebuild, a developer's laptop fails and costs half a day. The task has float and the repair cost is trivial. How should the project manager treat this?
options: Handle it as a day-to-day problem within tolerance
Escalate it to the sponsor as a formal project issue
Add it to the risk register as a new threat
Raise a change request to rebaseline the plan
A.why: The impact fits easily inside the PM's tolerances, so the PM simply deals with it. Only problems beyond tolerance are escalated as issues.

whyNot.1: Escalating a trivial problem wastes the sponsor's time and blurs what genuinely needs a decision.
whyNot.2: It has already happened, so it is not an uncertain future event for the risk register.
whyNot.3: Nothing in the baseline needs to change; the float absorbs the half day.

A.q: What is the main purpose of the ANALYSIS part of 'logging and analysis' in the issue process?
options: To decide who should be blamed for causing the problem
To record the issue so that it is not forgotten
To establish impact, urgency and possible options
To close the issue once the sponsor has decided
A.why: Analysis works out the impact on objectives, how urgent it is, its cause and the options, so a sound decision can be made at the right level.

whyNot.0: Issue management is about resolving problems, not assigning blame.
whyNot.1: Recording it is the logging part of the stage, not the analysis.
whyNot.3: Closure comes only after actions are complete and the issue is resolved.

B.q: A project manager must escalate an issue on a museum refurbishment. What should the escalation to the sponsor ideally contain?
options: The facts only, leaving the sponsor to find options
A fix the team has already put in place without approval
A request for the sponsor to run the issue log
The impact, the options and a recommended action
B.why: A good escalation explains the impact, sets out the realistic options and recommends one, so the sponsor can decide quickly.

whyNot.0: The PM is best placed to analyse options; passing on bare facts slows the decision.
whyNot.1: If the fix needed authority beyond the PM, implementing it before approval bypasses governance.
whyNot.2: The PM keeps the issue log; the sponsor makes the decision that is beyond the PM's authority.

B.q: An issue log entry reads: 'Owner: procurement lead. Action: sign the replacement supplier by 14 May. Status: open.' Which stage of the issue process does this entry mainly show?
options: Logging and analysis
Escalation
Assignment of actions
Closure
B.why: A named owner, a specific action and a deadline are the hallmarks of the assignment of actions stage.

whyNot.0: Logging and analysis records the issue and assesses its impact; it doesn't allocate the fix.
whyNot.1: Escalation raises the issue to the sponsor for a decision; this entry shows work after the decision.
whyNot.3: The status is still open, so the issue has not been closed.

B.q: A festival's risk register warned that the headline act might cancel. Two weeks out, the act cancels, and replacing them will exceed the budget tolerance. What has happened?
options: The risk has occurred and is now an issue
The risk should be re-analysed and kept open
It remains a risk until the festival takes place
It is a change request raised by the act's agent
B.why: The uncertainty is gone: the threat has occurred and breaches tolerance, so it is now an issue to be escalated and actioned.

whyNot.1: There is nothing left to analyse as a possibility; it has happened and needs action.
whyNot.2: A risk is uncertain. The cancellation is certain, so it is no longer a risk.
whyNot.3: A change request proposes a change to the baseline; the cancellation is a problem, not a request.

C.q: A project manager can see an issue will breach the cost tolerance, but waits a month hoping to recover the overspend before telling the sponsor. Why is this poor practice?
options: Issues must always be escalated within 24 hours
The sponsor's options shrink the longer it waits
Only the board, not the sponsor, may hear issues
An unescalated issue automatically becomes a risk
C.why: Prompt escalation keeps the most options open (funding, descoping, rescheduling). Delay hides the problem and narrows the choices.

whyNot.0: There is no universal 24-hour rule; the principle is to escalate promptly once tolerance is threatened.
whyNot.2: Issues are escalated first to the sponsor, who may refer them to the board if beyond their own authority.
whyNot.3: An issue never turns back into a risk; it has already happened.

C.q: On an agile app project, a developer says at the daily stand-up that the test environment is down and blocking work. It can be fixed well within the sprint. Who should normally deal with it first?
options: The sponsor, through a formal escalation report
The steering group, at the next decision gate
The change control board, via a change request
The team, as an impediment within the time box
C.why: In iterative working, blockers are raised at stand-ups and cleared by the team within the time box. Escalation is only needed if the fixed time or cost is threatened.

whyNot.0: It is within the team's capacity to fix, so formal escalation to the sponsor is unnecessary.
whyNot.1: Waiting for a decision gate would leave the team blocked; this is a quick, team-level fix.
whyNot.2: No change to scope, time or cost is being requested, so change control isn't involved.

C.q: On a linear project, the sponsor resolves an escalated issue by agreeing to remove a feature to absorb the extra cost. What should happen before the team acts on this?
options: The PM closes the issue and tells the team to stop
The change is assessed and the baseline updated
The issue is converted into a risk and monitored
The team decides informally which work to drop
C.why: Removing scope changes the baseline, so it goes through change control and the plans are updated, keeping everyone working to the same version.

whyNot.0: The issue is not resolved until the agreed actions are complete, so it can't be closed yet.
whyNot.2: The problem has happened; it is not an uncertain event to monitor.
whyNot.3: Informal descoping bypasses change control and leaves the baseline wrong.

reteach.title: Think of a wedding planner
reteach.question: A wedding planner has agreed a budget with the couple and can spend up to £500 extra without asking. Three weeks before the day, the caterer pulls out. What does the planner do?

blocks.body: The planner writes it down straight away and rings round: the best replacement costs £2,000 more. That is far beyond the £500 the planner may spend alone, so it is an issue. The planner phones the couple (the sponsors) with three options and a recommendation. The couple choose one. The planner then hands out actions: book the new caterer, update the menu cards, tell the venue. Only when the new caterer is confirmed and briefed is it ticked off.

steps.label:
Log and
analyse
steps.sub: Write it down; +£2,000 against a £500 limit

steps.label: Escalate
steps.sub: Call the couple with options and a recommendation

steps.label:
Assign
actions
steps.sub: Who books, who reprints, who tells the venue

steps.label: Close
steps.sub: Confirmed and briefed: tick it off

blocks.text: If the florist were 20 minutes late, the planner would just sort it out: that is a day-to-day problem within tolerance, not an issue for the couple.

explain.body: Two tests: it has happened (or is certain to), and it breaches, or is about to breach, the PM's delegated tolerances. Fail the first test and it is a risk. Fail the second and it is a day-to-day problem the PM handles.

test.q: Which situation is an issue rather than a risk?
options: A supplier might go bust before delivery next year
Planning consent could be refused next month
Key staff may resign when the merger is announced
The contractor quit yesterday, breaching tolerance
test.why: The contractor has already left and the impact breaches tolerance, so it is an issue needing escalation and action.

whyNot.0: 'Might go bust' is uncertain, so it is a risk.
whyNot.1: 'Could be refused' is uncertain, so it is a risk.
whyNot.2: 'May resign' is uncertain, so it is a risk.

explain.body: Log every issue in one place with a reference, date, description, cause, impact, priority, owner and status. Then analyse it: what does it do to time, cost, quality, scope and benefits, how urgent is it, what caused it, and what are the options? Good analysis makes for a quick, sound decision.

test.q: Why is an issue logged even when the project manager plans to escalate it straight away?
options: Logging transfers ownership of the issue to the sponsor
An issue can only be escalated if it was a risk
It creates a record that can be tracked to closure
Logging means the issue no longer needs analysis
test.why: The log is the single, auditable record: it lets the issue, its decision and its actions be tracked through to closure and reviewed later.

whyNot.0: Logging doesn't move ownership; the sponsor decides, and named owners carry out actions.
whyNot.1: Many issues were never identified as risks; they are escalated on their impact, not their history.
whyNot.3: Logging and analysis go together; recording it doesn't replace understanding its impact.

explain.body: Escalate when the issue needs authority the PM does not hold. It goes to the sponsor, who may provide funds, accept a delay, approve a scope change or, if the business case no longer stands, recommend closing the project. If it is beyond the sponsor's authority too, it goes up to the board or portfolio.

test.q: A PM's cost tolerance is ±£20,000. An issue will add £60,000, which is also beyond the sponsor's own spending authority. Where does the decision go?
options: The PM decides, using the project's contingency
The team leader decides, as it affects their own work
The supplier decides, as they caused the problem
The sponsor escalates it to the board or portfolio
test.why: Each level escalates what is beyond its authority. The sponsor can't approve it alone, so the board or portfolio decides.

whyNot.0: It breaches the PM's tolerance, so the PM can't decide it alone.
whyNot.1: Team leaders have even less authority than the PM.
whyNot.2: The supplier may have caused the problem, but the decision belongs to the project's governance.

explain.body: Once the decision is made, each action gets a named owner and a deadline. If the baseline changes, the change goes through change control. The PM tracks the actions and closes the issue only when it is resolved, recording any lesson (such as better supplier checks) for future projects.

test.q: Actions for an issue have been assigned and approved by the sponsor, but none are complete yet. Can the issue be closed?
options: Yes, the sponsor's decision ends the process
No, only once actions are done and it is resolved
Yes, provided it is moved to the risk register
No, issues stay open until the whole project closes
test.why: An issue is closed when it has been resolved, which means the assigned actions are complete and effective.

whyNot.0: A decision is not a resolution; the actions still need to be carried out.
whyNot.2: An issue has happened; moving it to the risk register would hide it.
whyNot.3: Issues are closed as soon as they are resolved, not held open to the end.
